The installer includes the plugin, and the app offers to install the AWS CLI for you on first start (checked against Amazon's digital signature). Install Download SSMConnect-Setup-x64.exe . Run it, accept the licence, and install. Windows asks for permission once. Leave Open the SSMConnect dashboard now ticked on the last page. Tip: to pin it to the taskbar, right-click the open SSMConnect window's taskbar button and choose Pin to taskbar . File > Create desktop shortcut adds a desktop icon. First run: the setup wizard The wizard has five short steps. The page on the right of each step explains why it is there. Requirements. Checks the AWS CLI and the Session Manager plugin. If one is missing, click Install missing components automatically . AWS account. Paste your company sign-in address (it is often pre-filled), sign in once in the browser, and choose a region. Every AWS account under the sign-in comes along automatically. Using access keys instead? There is a small link on the same page. Servers. SSMConnect lists your running servers and marks which ones SSM can reach. Tick the ones you want. SSH keys. Each Linux server is matched to its key file. Use Find key files on this PC , Search a folder... or Browse for a key... to help. Save. SSMConnect writes the sessions into PuTTY, WinSCP and MobaXterm and starts the tunnels. Connect Open PuTTY, WinSCP or MobaXterm and pick the session named SSC - your server name , or click PuTTY / WinSCP (Linux) or Remote Desktop (Windows) on the server's card in the dashboard. A card turns green only when the tunnel is really up. If it is not, the card says in plain words what is wrong. Copy files between servers Once

t: AWS accounts and organizations | SSMConnect docs
d: Sign in once for a company IAM Identity Center sign-in and see every AWS account under it. Add, rename and remove accounts in SSMConnect.
x: Home / Documentation / AWS accounts and organizations Get started Getting started with SSMConnect on Windows Dashboard guide Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Server types and tags Help and safety Troubleshooting Frequently asked questions Security For IT teams Extra feature Copy files between servers Linux edition SSMConnect for Linux Install and update on Linux Linux release notes Reference What is new in SSMConnect for Windows Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Updated 2026-10-22 3 min read Also on the GitHub wiki On this page Two words to know The account switcher Add an AWS account Manage accounts: rename or remove New organization accounts show up on rescan Sign in again Good to know Two words to know Sign-in (primary account): one company sign-in (AWS IAM Identity Center) or one set of access keys. Organization account: one AWS account inside a company sign-in. A company sign-in usually has several. SSMConnect finds all of them when you sign in, so you never add them one by one. The account switcher The pill in the top right of the dashboard shows the sign-in you are looking at. Click it to switch, add an account, or manage accounts. It lists sign-ins only , never the organizations under them. The window shows one sign-in at a time . Under it, servers are grouped by organization account. Switching is just a change of view. Connections of the other sign-ins keep running, and the summary and tray icon still cover everything. A row of chips under the status pills lists each organization account with its server count. Accounts with no servers yet are greyed. Add an AWS account AWS > Add AWS account (or Add AWS account... in the switcher) opens the setup wizard on one page: Paste your company sign-in address, for example https://yourcompany.awsapps.com/start . It is usually filled in for you. Click Sign in with AWS , then sign in and approve in the browser (up to 3 minutes). SSMConnect finds your accounts and roles and carries on to region and servers. Prefer access keys? Use the small Use access keys instead link. The keys are written only to your own ~/.aws/credentials , the same way the AWS CLI does it. Manage accounts: rename or remove AWS > Manage accounts... shows one collapsed line per sign-in. Click the arrow to see the organization accounts under it. Rename gives a sign-in or an organization a friendly name. It appears in the switcher, the headings and the wizard. The AWS profile name itself does not change. Leave the box empty to go back to the original name. Remove deletes the account's saved connections from SSMConnect and its login from this PC. Your PuTTY and WinSCP sessions and the servers in AWS are not touched. You can add the account again at any time. New organization accounts show up on rescan

t: Server types and tags | SSMConnect docs
d: How SSMConnect decides that a server is PROD, UAT or development from its AWS tags, and how to tag instances so the labels are right.
x: Home / Documentation / Server types and tags Get started Getting started with SSMConnect on Windows Dashboard guide Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Server types and tags Help and safety Troubleshooting Frequently asked questions Security For IT teams Extra feature Copy files between servers Linux edition SSMConnect for Linux Install and update on Linux Linux release notes Reference What is new in SSMConnect for Windows Accounts and servers Server types and tags Updated 2026-10-22 1 min read Also on the GitHub wiki On this page How it decides Tag your servers for the best result Servers saved before you tagged them SSMConnect shows what kind of server each one is (Production, UAT, Development, ...) as a small tag on the card. It reads this from your AWS tags , not from the server name. How it decides It looks at the server's tags, in this order: Environment , Env , Stage , Tier and similar names (any letter case, also keys ending in :environment or -env ). It normalises the value: Tag value (examples) Shown as prod , PRD , production , live PROD (red) pre-prod , preprod Pre-production uat UAT stage , staging Staging test , qa Test dev , development Development dr DR sandbox Sandbox internal Internal Only when a server has no such tag does SSMConnect fall back to guessing from the name, word by word. non-prod and pre-prod are never treated as production. Tag your servers for the best result Add an Environment tag to every instance, for example Environment = Production . It takes a minute in the AWS console, and it makes the PROD marker exact. Servers saved before you tagged them The type is stored when you save a server and refreshed from the last scan. After adding tags in AWS, run Servers > Scan for new or changed servers to pick them up. Previous AWS accounts and organizations Next Troubleshooting

PuTTY says "No supported authentication methods available" The server did not accept the key or user. From 2.0.2 SSMConnect tests the login before opening the tool and fixes the user and key by itself. If it asks for a key file, choose the .pem (or .ppk ) this server was created with. A key protected by a passphrase cannot be converted for PuTTY or WinSCP; use MobaXterm, or save it as a .ppk in PuTTYgen. "Your AWS sign-in has expired" Click the red AWS sign-in pill (or the Sign in button on the server card). Your browser opens; sign in and the pill turns green. AWS > Sign in again does the same. The AWS pill is red The sign-in of the account you are viewing has expired. Click the pill to sign in. Other accounts are checked separately when you switch to them. A card says Stopped The server failed 3 tries in a row, so SSMConnect stopped trying. Read the reason on the card, fix it, then click Sign in again (top right) to give every server 3 more tries. Sign-in window does not open my browser Pick the browser in the sign-in window, or click Open the window again . If the browser is not listed, SSMConnect uses the Windows default. The usage bars on a card show -- No usage reading yet. Click Refresh usage . If it stays empty, your AWS role is probably not allowed to run commands through SSM ( ssm:SendCommand ); hover a bar for the reason. Production servers are not read automatically (click Refresh usage ), and the Servers menu can switch automatic reading off or on. Sizes also need ec2:DescribeInstances , ec2:DescribeInstanceTypes and ec2:DescribeVolumes . A connection closed by itself Connections stay open until you click Stop connections or exit, and SSMConnect reopens a session that AWS ends. After 3 failed tries a card shows Stopped : read its message, then click Sign in again . Your administrators may also set an idle limit in AWS. A card is amber or red Read the message on the card. It says what to do: sign in, install a tool, start the connections, or free a port that is in use. "Port already in use" Another program uses that local port. Close it or restart SSMConnec

t: Security | SSMConnect docs
d: How SSMConnect keeps connections local, validates input, stores no secrets, protects converted keys and handles file transfer safely.
x: Home / Documentation / Security Get started Getting started with SSMConnect on Windows Dashboard guide Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Server types and tags Help and safety Troubleshooting Frequently asked questions Security For IT teams Extra feature Copy files between servers Linux edition SSMConnect for Linux Install and update on Linux Linux release notes Reference What is new in SSMConnect for Windows Help and safety Security Updated 2026-10-22 2 min read Also on the GitHub wiki On this page What it does for you What to know Reporting a security issue SSMConnect is built so that connecting is easy and nothing extra is exposed. What it does for you No open ports on your servers. Everything goes through AWS Systems Manager; port 22 can stay closed. Local only. Tunnels listen on 127.0.0.1 . If a tunnel port is ever found open to the network, SSMConnect closes that session and reports it. No impostors. A tunnel never starts on a port another program already uses, so nothing else can answer in place of your server and the dashboard cannot show a false green. Validated input. Every value read from the configuration (instance ID, account, region, ports, login) is checked before it reaches the AWS CLI, which is always started with an argument list, never a command-line string. Tied to the app. Sessions are closed when SSMConnect exits. No secrets kept. SSMConnect stores no password and no key of its own. A copied Windows password leaves the clipboard after 60 seconds. Access keys you type go only to your own ~/.aws/credentials , like the AWS CLI does. Safe edits. Before changing your AWS files or your MobaXterm settings, a .ssmconnect.bak copy is kept beside them. Your own sessions in PuTTY and WinSCP are never modified. Runs as you. Nothing runs as administrator or SYSTEM. Each Windows user has their own settings, tunnels and ~/.aws sign-in. File transfer stays on your PC. Files pass through your PC's memory in small blocks and are not saved to disk. The file window never works as root, and a sudo password you type is handed to sudo through a short-lived private helper file on the server that is removed when the window closes. Converted keys are locked down. The .ppk copies SSMConnect makes for PuTTY are readable only by your Windows user. Only AWS sign-in pages open. The sign-in window opens links on AWS's own domains only. Checked downloads. Updates are verified against the SHA-256 checksum published with the release. The AWS installers are checked against Amazon's digital signature and pinned by hash. What to know Another user logged in to the same PC at the same time can reach the local tunnel ports ( 127.0.0.1:2201 and up). They still need valid SSH credentials for the server, so the SSH login is what protects it. The installer

d: What servers and people need for SSMConnect: SSM Agent, instance roles, IAM permissions, pre-filled sign-in settings, tagging and unattended installs.
x: Home / Documentation / For IT teams Get started Getting started with SSMConnect on Windows Dashboard guide Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Server types and tags Help and safety Troubleshooting Frequently asked questions Security For IT teams Extra feature Copy files between servers Linux edition SSMConnect for Linux Install and update on Linux Linux release notes Reference What is new in SSMConnect for Windows Help and safety For IT teams Updated 2026-10-22 1 min read Also on the GitHub wiki On this page What each server needs What each person needs Pre-fill the company sign-in Tagging Unattended install and uninstall Verifying downloads Supported Windows What each server needs The SSM Agent running. An instance role that allows SSM, for example the AWS managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore . Network path from the instance to the SSM endpoints (internet access or VPC endpoints for ssm , ssmmessages and ec2messages ). What each person needs Permissions equivalent to: ec2:DescribeInstances ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation ssm:StartSession Access to Windows passwords (the Get password button) also needs ec2:GetPasswordData and the server's key file. Pre-fill the company sign-in On a PC that is part of your network, SSMConnect finds the IAM Identity Center address and region by itself, in this order: Settings you push: registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\SSMConnect values SsoStartUrl and SsoRegion (Group Policy or Intune), or %ProgramData%\SSMConnect\sso.json containing {"startUrl":"https://yourcompany.awsapps.com/start","region":"ap-south-1"} , or the environment variables SSMCONNECT_SSO_URL and SSMCONNECT_SSO_REGION . Existing ~/.aws/config settings. Sign-ins the AWS CLI already cached. A guess from the company domain, always shown for confirmation. Without one of the first three, nothing on the network announces the address, so a one-time policy or file is the dependable way. Tagging Ask teams to tag instances with Environment (Production, UAT, Development, ...). See Server Types and Tags . Unattended install and uninstall The setup file runs with /quiet . An uninstall run with /quiet keeps user settings unless you add RemoveSettings=1 . SSMConnect.Wizard.exe --cleanup removes only the saved sessions and settings of the current user. Verifying downloads Every release lists the SHA-256 of each file in SHA256SUMS.txt . Compare with Get-FileHash .\SSMConnect-Setup-x64.exe . Supported Windows 64-bit Windows 10 (1607+), Windows 11, Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022 and later with the desktop experience. Server Core has no screen for the setup window. t: Copy files between servers | SSMConnect docs
d: Once two servers are connected, copy files and folders from one to the other with two panes and a Copy button. Port 22 stays closed and the servers never need to reach each other.
x: Home / Documentation / Copy files between servers Get started Getting started with SSMConnect on Windows Dashboard guide Accounts and servers AWS accounts and organizations Server types and tags Help and safety Troubleshooting Frequently asked questions Security For IT teams Extra feature Copy files between servers Linux edition SSMConnect for Linux Install and update on Linux Linux release notes Reference What is new in SSMConnect for Windows Extra feature Copy files between servers Updated 2026-10-22 4 min read Also on the GitHub wiki On this page Copy a file in four steps How the data travels Switch to another user (sudo) What it protects you from Good to know If something does not work Related An extra feature. SSMConnect is mainly about connecting to your servers: see Getting Started . Once two servers are connected, this window lets you copy between them. Move files from one AWS server to another with two panes and a Copy button, while port 22 stays closed on both. No S3 bucket, no scp commands, no bastion host, and the two servers never have to reach each other. Open it from Servers > File transfer: browse and copy files... in the dashboard (it also opens from a server card's tools when you want to move files). The window is titled Copy files between servers . Copy a file in four steps Pick the organization at the top (your company sign-in). Both sides list only its servers, because only servers of one sign-in can be linked. Pick a server on the left and one on the right. Each pane starts with Select the server to connect and connects to nothing until you choose. SSMConnect then signs in as the server's default user with its saved key. There is nothing to type. Browse and select. Open folders on either side, then select one or more files or folders. Folders are copied with everything inside them. Press Copy. Use Copy ▶ to send the selection from left to right, or ◀ Copy for the other direction. The bar shows progress and Stop cancels. How the data travels Server A -> SSM tunnel -> your PC -> SSM tunnel -> Server B Each server is reached through an AWS Systems Manager tunnel that SSMConnect already keeps open on your PC, so no inbound port is opened on either server. Files are read from one server and written to the other in small blocks as they pass through your PC. Nothing is saved on your disk. The servers do not need a network path to each other. They can be in different VPCs, subnets or AWS accounts, as long as both belong to the same sign-in organization. Everything is carried over SSH (SFTP) inside the SSM session. Switch to another user (sudo) Some files belong to another account, for example a web server's user. In either pane, pick or type the user and click Switch user . d: A native Linux app for connecting to AWS servers over SSM with port 22 closed: dashboard, Terminal, Files over SFTP, Remote Desktop and signed packages.

Same idea as on Windows: connect to your AWS servers with port 22 closed, no bastion host, no VPN, no infrastructure knowledge needed. ssh ssc-web-1 -> 127.0.0.1:2201 -> aws ssm start-session -> your server (port 22) What you get A native desktop app (GTK 4 and libadwaita, written in Rust, light and dark themes). Not Wine, not Mono, not Electron. The same dashboard: one card per server, a live status dot, PROD / UAT tags from your AWS tags, Start / Stop / Restart, accounts and organizations. Terminal opens ssh to the server. Files opens the server's folders over SFTP in your file manager (or the sftp client in a terminal). Remote Desktop and Get password for Windows servers (Remmina or FreeRDP). Every server also gets a short name for the command line: ssh ssc-<server-name> , scp , rsync , VS Code Remote-SSH. A Preferences window with every setting in plain words, and a Server identities window to confirm each server's SSH identity (no editing of known_hosts by hand). One installer file ( .bin ) with a wizard. It fetches what it needs from each tool's own source, never bundles third-party tools, updates an existing install in place and keeps your servers and settings . Your system (vendor-supported releases, checked 2026-10) Use Fedora 43 and 44 the .rpm RHEL, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux 10 the .rpm openSUSE Leap 16.0 and Tumbleweed the .rpm Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Linux Mint 22 the .deb Debian 13 the .deb RHEL, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux 8 and 9 the Flatpak Ubuntu 22.04, Linux Mint 21 the Flatpak Debian 12 the Flatpak The native packages and the .bin installer need GTK 4.12+, libadwaita 1.5+ and glibc 2.39+, which the first five rows ship. The older releases in the last three rows cannot run them, so the Flatpak brings its own GTK and libadwaita (the GNOME runtime). Releases a vendor no longer supports (for example Fedora 42, Debian 11, openSUSE Leap 15.6) are not covered. Flatpak (needs the flatpak package, which is in the standard repositories of all three families; on Ubuntu 22.04 and Mint 21 it is already there or one sudo apt install flatpak away): flatpak install --user https://poonchezhian.github.io/ssmconnect/ssmconnect.flatpakref flatpak run io.github.poonchezhian.SSMConnect flatpak update brings new versions. t: Connect to an EC2 server over SSM without opening port 22 | SSMConnect blog
d: How to reach your AWS servers with PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm or Remote Desktop while port 22 stays closed, and how SSMConnect sets it all up in one short wizard.
x: You have an EC2 server. You want a terminal on it. Somebody, wisely, closed port 22. This is the situation SSMConnect was built for: you still get PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm or Remote Desktop, and the server keeps every inbound port closed. ## Why port 22 is closed, and why that is good An open SSH port is reachable by the whole internet, and it is attacked all day long. Many teams close it and use AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager instead. The server's SSM Agent calls out to AWS, and AWS carries your connection back over that existing channel. No inbound port, no bastion host, no VPN. The catch is that the usual way to use it is a long command line, plus a plugin, plus a port number you have to remember. If you are a developer who just wants to log in, that is a lot of plumbing. If you want to understand it first, read [SSM port forwarding explained](/blog/ssm-port-forwarding-explained/). ## What SSMConnect does for you SSMConnect is a free Windows app (and a Linux app) that does the plumbing: 1. **Finds your servers.** Sign in once with your company sign-in and it lists the running servers in every AWS account under it, and marks which ones SSM can reach. 2. **Opens one tunnel per server.** Each server gets its own local port on `127.0.0.1`. The tunnels run as you, not as an administrator, and restart by themselves if they drop. 3. **Sets up your tools.** Linux servers get saved sessions called `SSC - <server name>` in PuTTY, WinSCP and MobaXterm. Windows servers open in Remote Desktop. 4. **Tells you the truth about the connection.** A server card turns green only when its tunnel is really up. If something is wrong, the card says what, in plain words. ## Your first connection in five steps 1. [Download SSMConnect for Windows](https://github.com/poonchezhian/ssmconnect/releases/latest/download/SSMConnect-Setup-x64.exe) and run the installer. It adds the AWS CLI and the Session Manager plugin if they are missing. 2. In the setup wizard, paste your company sign-in address and sign in once in the browser. 3. Tick the servers you want. 4. Point each Linux server at its key file. **Find key files on this PC** does most of the work. 5. Save. The tunnels start, and the dashboard shows your servers. From then on, open PuTTY, WinSCP or MobaXterm and pick the session called `SSC - your server name`, or click **PuTTY**, **WinSCP** or **Remote Desktop** on the server's card. ## What you need on the AWS side SSMConnect cannot give a server something it does not have. For a server to be reachable, it needs the SSM Agent running and an instance role such as `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore`. Your own AWS role needs `ec2:DescribeInstances`, `ssm:DescribeInstanceInformation` and `ssm:StartSession`. If a server shows up as not reachable, [For IT teams](/docs/for-

t: How to copy files between EC2 servers when port 22 is closed | SSMConnect blog
d: Four ways to move files from one EC2 server to another when SSH is closed and you only have AWS Systems Manager: S3, manual port forwarding, rsync, and a two-pane window in SSMConnect.
x: Closing port 22 is one of the best security decisions you can make for an EC2 server. It also breaks the thing every developer does without thinking: `scp app.tar.gz other-server:/tmp/`. With no inbound SSH there is no `other-server` to reach, and the two servers often cannot see each other anyway. If you reach your servers through AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager, you still have good options. This post compares four of them, shows the exact commands, and says honestly when each one is the right pick. ## The problem in one picture You are signed in to AWS. Both servers are online in Systems Manager. You can open a shell on each. You need `app-2.4.1.tar.gz` to move from `web-prod-01` to `app-uat-02`. Session Manager gives you a shell and port forwarding. It does not give you a copy command between two servers. So the file has to travel some other way. ## Option 1: S3 as the hand-off Put the file in a bucket from server A and pull it from server B. ``` # on server A aws s3 cp /var/www/releases/app-2.4.1.tar.gz s3://my-handoff-bucket/tmp/ # on server B aws s3 cp s3://my-handoff-bucket/tmp/app-2.4.1.tar.gz /home/ec2-user/incoming/ ``` This is the right answer for large files, repeated jobs and anything that needs an audit trail. The costs are setup and housekeeping: a bucket, an instance role on both servers that allows the bucket, two commands per file, and a clean-up step so the file does not sit in S3 forever. For a quick one-off it is a lot of ceremony. ## Option 2: Two port-forwarded tunnels and scp through your PC Open one tunnel per server, then copy down and back up. ``` aws ssm start-session --target i-0aaa1111bbbb2222c ^ --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession ^ --parameters "portNumber=22,localPortNumber=2201" aws ssm start-session --target i-0ddd3333eeee4444f ^ --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession ^ --parameters "portNumber=22,localPortNumber=2202" ``` Each command stays running in its own window. Then, from a third window: ``` scp -i keyA.pem -P 2201 ubuntu@127.0.0.1:/var/www/releases/app-2.4.1.tar.gz . scp -i keyB.pem -P 2202 app-2.4.1.tar.gz ec2-user@127.0.0.1:/home/ec2-user/incoming/ ``` It works, and it needs nothing in AWS beyond SSM. The price is attention: two terminals, two ports to remember, two key files, the right user for each server, and a copy of the file on your disk in the middle that you must delete. ## Option 3: rsync over a forwarded port For repeated syncs of a folder, rsync over the same kind of tunnel is hard to beat, because it only sends what changed. It has the same set-up cost as option 2 and the same two-hop shape when the destination is another server. Use it when you sync the same tree again and again. ## Option 4: Two panes and a Copy button [SSMConnect](/) keeps the SSM tunnels open fo

t: What is new in SSMConnect 2.0: connections that stay open and a calmer dashboard | SSMConnect blog
d: A tour of SSMConnect 2.0 to 2.0.5 for Windows: connect-all with keep-alive, login checks before PuTTY opens, usage bars, a file window that matches the dashboard, and a scrolling grid for large fleets.
x: SSMConnect 2.0 is a bigger change than the number suggests. Here is what changed between 2.0.0 and 2.0.5, and why. ## Everything connects, and stays connected 2.0.0 opened connections on demand and closed them when idle. In use, that turned out to be one thing too many to think about. From 2.0.1 every server connects when SSMConnect starts (or after you sign in) and stays connected until you click **Stop connections** or exit. If AWS ends a session, SSMConnect quietly opens the next one. A server that fails three tries in a row shows **Stopped** and waits for you to click **Sign in again**. A connection that comes up but drops within 30 seconds now counts as a failed try, so it cannot loop forever. ## The login is checked before PuTTY opens A green card only meant that the tunnel was up. If the key or user was wrong, PuTTY still said "No supported authentication methods available". Since 2.0.2, before PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm or the file window opens, SSMConnect finds the key that belongs to the server, tests which login user it accepts, saves what works and refreshes the saved sessions. If no key fits, it asks you once for the right key file. In 2.0.4 this became gentler on your servers: when the operating system is known only its own default user is tried, and combinations a server refused are not retried for ten minutes. ## Usage at a glance Each card shows CPU, memory and disk as three small bars with an icon and a percentage, green under 60, amber to 85 and red above that. In 2.0.5 they sit on the same line as the status, which makes the cards shorter. Reading usage runs a short read-only command through SSM, so in 2.0.4 production servers are read only when you click **Refresh usage**, and the **Servers** menu has a switch to turn automatic reading off. ## A file window that matches The window for [copying files between servers](/file-transfer/) now shares the dashboard's look: a soft backdrop and glass cards. Both panes start with "Select the server to connect" and connect to nothing until you pick. ## A grid that scrolls If you have a dozen servers, the cards used to drop to fewer columns and cut off the last row. 2.0.5 places the cards itself, so the columns match the window and the list always scrolls. ## Small things that matter - Updates replace SSMConnect in place and the app has a fixed Windows identity, so a taskbar pin on Windows 10 survives an update. - The converted PuTTY keys are readable only by your Windows user. - The sign-in window only opens links on AWS's own domains. The full list for every version is in [What's new](/docs/whats-new/). [Download SSMConnect for Windows](https://github.com/poonchezhian/ssmconnect/releases/latest/download/SSMConnect-Setup-x64.exe) and update from inside the app with **Help > Check for updates**

t: Is it safe to copy files between servers through your PC? | SSMConnect blog
d: How SSMConnect's file transfer is built: SSH inside the SSM tunnel, streaming through memory, no root, a private sudo helper, and the limits you should know about.
x: When a file travels from one server to another through your computer, a sensible person asks three questions: who can see it on the way, what is left behind, and what can the tool do on my servers? Here are the answers for the file window in [SSMConnect](/), including the limits. ## Who can see the file on the way The path is server A, then the SSM tunnel, then your PC, then the second SSM tunnel, then server B. - Both hops are carried by AWS Systems Manager, over the connection each server's SSM Agent already makes out to AWS. No inbound port is opened. - The tunnel ends on `127.0.0.1` on your PC. SSMConnect checks that tunnels listen only on your own computer and closes a tunnel if it ever finds one reachable from the network. - Inside the tunnel, the file window talks SSH to each server (SFTP for the default user, sudo-run commands after Switch user). So the content is protected by SSH between your PC and each server, on top of what AWS does. One honest note: another user signed in to the same PC at the same moment could reach a local tunnel port. They would still need valid SSH credentials for the server, which is what protects it. ## What is left behind - **On your PC:** nothing. The program reads a block from the source, writes it to the destination, and repeats. The blocks live in memory only while they pass through. No temporary copy is saved to disk. - **On the servers:** the copied file at the destination, and nothing else. If you use **Switch user** with a sudo password, that password is handed to sudo through a short-lived private helper file that is removed when you close the window. - **In the log:** the names of items that failed and the reason, for troubleshooting. Contents are never logged. ## What the tool can do on your servers - It signs in with the server's saved key as the server's default user. SSMConnect stores no password and no key of its own. It points at the key file you already have. - It never works as root. The window refuses the name `root`, and it also refuses any account that turns out to have root rights (uid 0). - Acting as another user is done with `sudo -u`, so what that user may do is decided by the server's own sudo rules. - Before replacing anything, it lists the names that already exist and waits for you to confirm. - Both servers must belong to one sign-in organization. The window will not copy to a server outside it. ## The limits, stated plainly - The window moves data through your PC, so it is as fast as your connection to AWS allows, and not suited to hundreds of gigabytes. - There is no resume. An interrupted file starts again. - It is for Linux servers over SSH. Windows servers use Remote Desktop. - SSMConnect is an early release for Windows. The Windows installer is not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen

t: SSM port forwarding explained for developers | SSMConnect blog
d: What AWS Systems Manager port forwarding does, why your tools connect to 127.0.0.1, and how one tunnel per server lets PuTTY, WinSCP and Remote Desktop work with no open ports.
x: If you are a developer and not an infrastructure person, "SSM port forwarding" sounds like something to leave to someone else. It is actually one idea, and once you have it the rest of Session Manager stops being mysterious. ## The idea Your PC starts a small program that listens on a port on your own computer, for example `2201`. Anything that connects to `127.0.0.1:2201` is carried, through AWS Systems Manager, to a port on your server, usually port 22 for SSH or 3389 for Remote Desktop. The server never needed an open inbound port. It called out to AWS when its SSM Agent started, and AWS carries your traffic over that existing connection. ``` PuTTY -> 127.0.0.1:2201 -> AWS Systems Manager -> your server, port 22 ``` ## The command behind it ``` aws ssm start-session --target i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 ^ --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession ^ --parameters "portNumber=22,localPortNumber=2201" ``` - `--target` is the instance ID of the server. - `portNumber` is the port on the server you want to reach. - `localPortNumber` is the port that opens on your PC. The command keeps running. While it runs, the tunnel exists. Press Ctrl+C and it is gone. It needs the AWS CLI and the Session Manager plugin installed on your PC, and your AWS identity must be allowed `ssm:StartSession` on that instance. ## Why tools connect to 127.0.0.1 After the command starts, your server looks like it is on your own computer, at `127.0.0.1` with the local port you chose. So in PuTTY you type host `127.0.0.1` and port `2201`. In WinSCP the same. In Remote Desktop, `127.0.0.1:3390`. The tool does not know about AWS at all. ## One tunnel per server Each server needs its own local port, because a port can lead to only one place. Server one on 2201, server two on 2202, and so on. This is the part people forget, and the reason a spreadsheet of ports appears in so many teams. ## What can go wrong - **TargetNotConnected:** the SSM Agent is not running, the instance has no role that allows Systems Manager, or it cannot reach the Systems Manager endpoints. - **Port already in use:** another program, or an older tunnel, already uses that local port. Choose another. - **The session ends by itself:** AWS closes idle sessions after a limit your administrators set in the Session Manager preferences, 20 minutes by default. - **The login is refused:** the tunnel only carries the connection. SSH still checks your key and user name, for example `ec2-user` or `ubuntu`. ## Where SSMConnect fits [SSMConnect](/) does the bookkeeping: it signs you in, finds the servers that are ready, picks a free local port for each, keeps the tunnels open, restarts a tunnel if AWS ends it, and saves sessions in PuTTY, WinSCP and MobaXterm. It also uses the same tunnels for [copying files between two servers](/fi

t: About SSMConnect: connect to AWS servers over SSM with port 22 closed
d: How SSMConnect works, what you need, how it compares with doing it by hand, and how it keeps connections safe. Free and open source for Windows and Linux.
x: Home / About About SSMConnect Connect to your AWS servers over SSM. Leave port 22 closed. SSMConnect finds your EC2 servers, opens secure tunnels through AWS Systems Manager, and sets up PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm and Remote Desktop for you. It is written for developers who just want to connect, not for infrastructure specialists. Download for Windows Download for Linux Getting started The same connection, with and without the typing Reaching a server over Session Manager by hand means a long command, a local port to remember and a manual session in your SSH client. SSMConnect runs that command for you and saves the result as a session you can reopen. By hand, for every server $ aws sso login --profile prod $ aws ssm start-session \ --target i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \ --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSession \ --parameters '{"portNumber":["22"],"localPortNumber":["2222"]}' \ --profile prod # then: PuTTY, host 127.0.0.1, port 2222, key file... With SSMConnect Windows click Connect , PuTTY opens Linux click Connect , then Terminal or $ ssh ssc-web-prod The tunnel, the local port and the saved session or ssh name are handled for you. How it works Sign in Click Sign in. Your browser opens your company sign-in page (AWS IAM Identity Center), or you can use access keys. A small status line shows which accounts are signed in. Find your servers SSMConnect scans your accounts and lists the servers that are ready for Session Manager. A server that is not ready is flagged with a plain explanation of what is missing. Connect Press Connect. A tunnel opens on your own computer and your tool starts. On Windows that is PuTTY for SSH, WinSCP or MobaXterm for files and Remote Desktop for Windows servers. SSMConnect finds your EC2 servers, opens secure tunnels through AWS Systems Manager, and sets up PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm and Remote Desktop for you. No bastion host, no VPN, and no infrastructure knowledge needed. The Linux app does the same job with a native look. What it does Main job Connect with the tools you know One short wizard finds your servers and opens a tunnel for each. PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm and Remote Desktop are set up for you, and a card turns green only when the connection is really up. Latest post · 22 October 2026 Connect to an EC2 server over SSM without opening port 22 3 min read Permalink You have an EC2 server. You want a terminal on it. Somebody, wisely, closed port 22. This is the situation SSMConnect was built for: you still get PuTTY, WinSCP, MobaXterm or Remote Desktop, and the server keeps every inbound port closed. Why port 22 is closed, and why that is good An open SSH port is reachable by the whole internet, and it is attacked all day long. Many teams close it and use AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager instead. The server's SSM Agent calls out to AWS, and AWS carries your connection back over that existing channel. No inbound port, no bastion host, no VPN. The catch is that the usual way to use it is a long command line, plus a plugin, plus a port number you have to remember. If you are a developer who just wants to log in, that is a lot of plumbing. If you want to understand it first, read SSM port forwarding explained . What SSMConnect does for you SSMConnect is a free Windows app (and a Linux app) that does the plumbing: Finds your servers. Sign in once with your company sign-in and it lists the running servers in every AWS account under it, and marks which ones SSM can reach. Opens one tunnel per server. Each server gets its own local port on 127.0.0.1 . The tunnels run as you, not as an administrator, and restart by themselves if they drop. Sets up your tools.
